reason: The sources provide rich, verified details across multiple independent sites regarding hypervelocity stars, specific record-holders like S5-HVS1, and their ejection mechanisms.
story: Deep in the center of the Milky Way lurks Sagittarius A*, a four-million-solar-mass black hole. Around five million years ago, a binary star system wandered too close to this gravitational trap. Through a violent three-body disruption known as the Hills mechanism, the monster captured one star and hurled the other outward like a cosmic bullet. Today, that banished outcast—cataloged as S5-HVS1—is hurtling through space at nearly four million miles per hour, or over 1,700 kilometers per second. That is more than triple the velocity required to break free from the Milky Way's gravitational pull. Tracked by astronomers using sky surveys and the Gaia space telescope, S5-HVS1 is the cleanest confirmed ejection from our galactic center. With its trajectory pointing straight into the void, this lone star is doomed to wander the empty wastes of intergalactic space forever.
angle: The Milky Way's central black hole slingshotted a star at nearly four million miles per hour—fast enough to fling it completely out of our galaxy forever.

claims.claim: S5-HVS1 travels at an extraordinary velocity of approximately 1,700 to 1,755 km/s (nearly 4 million mph).
S5-HVS1 is an A-type main-sequence star.
S5-HVS1 was discovered through the Southern Stellar Stream Spectroscopic Survey (S5).
The discovery of S5-HVS1 was led by astronomer Sergey Koposov.
S5-HVS1 is located in the southern constellation Grus (the Crane).
S5-HVS1 is situated roughly 29,000 light-years away from Earth.
The backward trajectory of S5-HVS1 traces directly to Sagittarius A*, the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole.
S5-HVS1 was kicked out of the galactic center approximately 4.8 to 5 million years ago.
Hypervelocity stars travel fast enough to exceed the galaxy's escape velocity, unbinding them from the Milky Way into intergalactic space.
The Hills mechanism, proposed in 1988, describes how a binary star system is disrupted by a central black hole, capturing one star and hurling the other away at high speed.
The first hypervelocity star was discovered in 2005 by astronomer Warren Brown.
Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy, has a mass of approximately 4 million solar masses.
The diameter of the Milky Way's disk is approximately 100,000 light-years.
The escape velocity required to leave the Milky Way from the Sun's vicinity is roughly 500 to 550 km/s.
Astrometry data from the European Space Agency's Gaia spacecraft has been used to trace and confirm hypervelocity star paths.
The hypervelocity star US 708 hurtles through space at approximately 1,200 km/s.

disputed: Origin of all hypervelocity stars: Earlier models assumed all hypervelocity stars originated at the central supermassive black hole, but stars like LAMOST-HVS1 and US 708 originated in the disk or from binary supernova detonations. Scripts should specify that while Sagittarius A* is the primary engine, other ejection mechanisms exist.

Classification of US 708: S4 identifies US 708 as a helium-rich subdwarf, S5 and S7 describe it as a white dwarf, and S6 calls it an O-type star. Scripts should describe it generally as an extreme high-speed star or avoid specifying its stellar type.

Birthplace of HE 0437-5439: Early studies suggested it came from the Large Magellanic Cloud, but Hubble astrometry later traced its trajectory back to the Milky Way center. Scripts should present the Large Magellanic Cloud origin as an earlier hypothesis resolved by Hubble.
